strengths: Combining Stein control functionals with multilevel differences is a useful approach to expensive integration, including integration under unnormalized posterior densities.
The sample-split estimator has a clear unbiasedness argument under appropriate independence and Stein conditions, and the paper derives an explicit allocation rule under its cost model.
The integration experiments report improvements over relevant MC, MLMC, CF, and MLBQ baselines. Repeated runs and kernel and sampling-design ablations provide useful empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The main neural-network experiments are not reconciled with the estimator definition. Appendix D.5 reports one sample for MLCFRG. With one sample, Equation (11) reduces exactly to the raw function difference, independently of the kernel; the sample-split estimator instead requires additional fitting samples. Unless additional data are used but unreported, these experiments cannot demonstrate control-functional variance reduction. The implemented estimator and sample accounting require clarification.

The efficiency claims lack end-to-end computational evidence. The budgets emphasize sampling and function evaluation without demonstrating the contribution of kernel construction, hyperparameter fitting, and cubic matrix solves. These costs could matter substantially at the reported subsecond budgets. Neural-network comparisons primarily use iteration counts rather than elapsed time.

The variational-inference evaluation covers one subsampled UCI dataset and small networks. Against the strongest baseline, MLMCRG, test log-likelihood is essentially tied in Table 5 (-388.34 versus -388.42) and slightly worse in Table 6 (-386.57 versus -386.27). This does not establish a consistent predictive advantage. A single-level control-functional gradient baseline is also missing.

The theoretical guarantees cover substantially narrower settings than the experiments. A8's finite global fill distance cannot hold on the unbounded Gaussian domains used experimentally, and Theorem 3.2 does not directly cover MCMC sampling or the biased simplified estimator. Proposition 3.4 controls fresh conditional noise; the claimed extension to the full adaptive optimization trajectory needs an argument accounting for dependence on recycled gradient samples.

The theoretical novelty is limited: the variance bound applies existing single-level CF bounds to telescoping increments, and allocation follows standard constrained optimization. The proposed allocation is validated only on a constructed kernel example; practical integration experiments reuse MLMC allocations. The paper does not establish when fidelity refinement guarantees the RKHS norm decay needed for an advantage over single-level CF.

Appendix C.1 contains an incorrect multidimensional Matérn mixed-derivative formula. At coincident inputs, the mixed trace should equal 5dσ²/(3λ²), whereas the displayed expression gives 5σ²/(3λ²). This could be a transcription error, but the implementation must be checked because correct derivatives are necessary for the Stein-kernel construction.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified in the manuscript, including numerical fidelity step sizes and reference-integral construction for the ODE and Lotka–Volterra experiments, and the exact neural-network data subsampling and split. These omissions make the reported integration errors and predictive comparisons difficult to independently assess.
